title: 2 Samuel 17:1–14
context: With David in flight from Jerusalem, Absalom hears two counsels. Ahithophel, whose advice was regarded like an oracle from God (16:23), urges an immediate strike to kill David alone. Hushai, sent back by David to frustrate that counsel (15:32-34), persuades Absalom to wait and gather all Israel. The narrator explains the outcome: the LORD had ordained the defeat of Ahithophel’s good counsel, answering David’s prayer in 15:31. Both traditions find the contrast in 17:14 without making it a new key contrast; the same question of how God’s agency relates to human decisions is treated as a key contrast at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Moreover Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David tonight.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel proposes to pursue David that very night with twelve thousand men. Arminian readers note the shrewdness of a plan that sees the value of speed, and the moral weight of a trusted counselor who has freely turned against the king he once served.
verses.reformedNotes: Ahithophel’s counsel was esteemed as if one inquired of God (16:23), which makes his betrayal all the more serious. Reformed readers see the narrative setting up a contest between the wisest human strategy and the purpose of God.

verses.text: I will come on him while he is weary and exhausted, and will make him afraid. All the people who are with him will flee. I will strike the king only,
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel plans to come on David while he is weary and to strike the king only. Arminian readers note the cold precision of a plan aimed at one life, and the way political ambition reduces a person to an obstacle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the plan is militarily sound: kill the king, and the war ends. The danger to David is real, which makes God’s intervention in 17:14 all the more striking.

verses.text: and I will bring back all the people to you. The man whom you seek is as if all returned. All the people shall be in peace.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel promises that all the people will return to Absalom in peace once David is dead. Arminian readers see how a promise of peace can be used to justify violence against an innocent person.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the hollow peace Ahithophel offers, built on the death of God’s anointed. True peace for Israel could not come through rebellion against the king God had chosen.

verses.text: The saying pleased Absalom well, and all the elders of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The plan pleases Absalom and all the elders of Israel. Arminian readers note how quickly leaders can agree on a course that serves their ambitions, without asking whether it honors God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the counsel seemed settled, with broad approval. The narrator lets readers feel how close David came to ruin before God turned events.

verses.text: Then Absalom said, “Now call Hushai the Archite also, and let’s hear likewise what he says.”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom calls Hushai to hear his view as well. Arminian readers see a free decision by Absalom that opens the door to a different outcome, one with large consequences for him and for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God at work in Absalom’s seemingly ordinary choice to seek a second opinion. Providence often moves through decisions that appear routine to those who make them.

verses.text: When Hushai had come to Absalom, Absalom spoke to him, saying, “Ahithophel has spoken like this. Shall we do what he says? If not, speak up.”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom asks Hushai whether they should follow Ahithophel’s advice, and invites him to speak up if not. Arminian readers note that Absalom genuinely weighs the options, and so bears responsibility for the choice he makes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Absalom asks David’s loyal friend for advice. Hushai’s presence in Absalom’s council is itself part of the answer to David’s prayer (15:31-34).

verses.text: Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai says Ahithophel’s counsel this time is not good. Arminian readers note the careful wording, which concedes Ahithophel’s usual wisdom while challenging this one plan, a skillful appeal to Absalom’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Hushai acting as David’s agent in a dangerous position. His words are a means God uses to overturn counsel that the narrator itself calls good in 17:14.

verses.text: Hushai said moreover, “You know your father and his men, that they are mighty men, and they are fierce in their minds, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Your father is a man of war, and will not lodge with the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai describes David and his men as fierce and dangerous when cornered. Arminian readers note how he plays on Absalom’s fear and memory of his father’s reputation as a warrior.
verses.reformedNotes: The image of a bear robbed of her cubs appears also in Proverbs 17:12 and Hosea 13:8. Reformed readers see Hushai’s vivid language working on Absalom’s imagination in the service of God’s purpose.

verses.text: Behold, he is now hidden in some pit, or in some other place. It will happen, when some of them have fallen at the first, that whoever hears it will say, ‘There is a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom!’
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai warns that David is hidden somewhere, and an early loss would spread panic among Absalom’s followers. Arminian readers see a persuasive appeal to the uncertainties of war and the fragility of morale.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Hushai’s argument exaggerates the risks, yet it proves convincing. They see God turning a plausible human argument to accomplish what he had determined.

verses.text: Even he who is valiant, whose heart is as the heart of a lion, will utterly melt; for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and those who are with him are valiant men.
verses.arminianNotes: Even the bravest will melt, Hushai says, because all Israel knows David’s might. Arminian readers note how fear of an enemy’s strength can weaken resolve, a theme common in Israel’s story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the lion-hearted language that recalls David’s own reputation. The argument appeals to Absalom’s insecurity about his father, a weakness God uses. David’s fame becomes a weapon in Hushai’s mouth.

verses.text: But I counsel that all Israel be gathered together to you, from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude; and that you go to battle in your own person.
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai counsels gathering all Israel from Dan to Beersheba, with Absalom leading in person. Arminian readers see flattery that appeals to Absalom’s vanity and desire for glory, which he freely embraces.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase as the sand by the sea recalls the promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Reformed readers find it ironic that this promise language is used to rally Israel against the king God chose.

verses.text: So we will come on him in some place where he will be found, and we will light on him as the dew falls on the ground, then we will not leave so much as one of him and of all the men who are with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai pictures the army falling on David like dew on the ground, leaving no one alive. Arminian readers note the grand imagery that makes delay sound like strength rather than hesitation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plan’s appeal lying in its scale. The delay it requires gives David the time he needs to escape, which is exactly what God intends.

verses.text: Moreover, if he has gone into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will draw it into the river, until there isn’t one small stone found there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai claims that if David enters a city, Israel will drag it into the river with ropes. Arminian readers see deliberate exaggeration meant to impress and reassure Absalom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the absurd boast that a whole city could be pulled down with ropes. That such counsel prevails shows that Absalom’s judgment is being turned by a higher hand.

verses.text: Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil on Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom and the men of Israel prefer Hushai’s counsel, for the LORD had ordained to defeat Ahithophel’s good counsel. Arminian readers see God working through Absalom’s free choice and his vanity, answering David’s prayer (15:31) without forcing Absalom against his own desires.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign ordination stated plainly: the LORD had ordained this outcome to bring evil on Absalom. They see God governing even the decisions of his enemies, while Absalom remains fully responsible for his rebellion.
